la:num:tertius.html:
tertĭus, a, um,
num. ord. adj. [ter], the third.
Adj.: vos duo eritis, atque amica tua erit tecum tertia,: tres video sententias ferri: unam, etc. ... alteram, etc. ... tertiam ut, etc.,; cf. ; : sic disserunt: si quod sit in obscenitate flagitium, id aut in re esse aut in verbo: nihil esse tertium,; cf. : annus,: tertio illo anno,: mancipia venibant Saturnalibus tertiis,i.e. on the third day of the Saturnalia,: ab Jove tertius Ajax,the third in descent, greatgrandson of Jupiter,: per tertia numina juro,i.e. by the infernal gods,: regna,the infernal regions,: tertius e nobis,i.e. one of us three,: tertios creari (censores),: tertius dies est,it is two days since,: syllaba ab eā tertia,: diebus tertiis,every three days,. —
Substt.
tertĭae, ārum, f. (sc. partes).
A third part: miscentur argento tertiae aeris Cyprii,; : cum ad tertias subsederit coctura,; ; : duae tertiae partes,two thirds,.—*
The third part in a play: Spinther secundarum, tertiarumque Pamphilus,. —
Tertĭus, ii, m., and Tertĭa, ae, f., proper names. The latter in a sarcastic pun: Tertiā deductā (after a third was deducted, or after Tertia was seduced), Cic. ap. ; .—Adv.
tertĭō.
For the third time: non hercle veniam tertio,: ille iterum, ille tertio pecuniam dedit,: sanguis mittendus est iterum tertioque,, fin.: cui ter proditae patriae: semel cum, etc. ... iterum cum, etc. ... tertio hodie, etc.,; tertio consules esse, ; cf. .—*
In the third place, thirdly: haec spectans, etc. ... simul, ut, etc. ... tertio, ut, etc.,.—
Three times (post-class.): parietes tertio obducere,; Treb. Gall. 17. —
tertĭum, for the third time: nemo est quin saepe jactans Venerium jaciat aliquando, non numquam etiam iterum ac tertium,: veniunt iterum atque tertium, Cato ap. P.: idque iterum tertiumque,: consules creati Q. Fabius Vibulanus tertium et L. Cornelius Maluginensis,; : mori consulem tertium oportuit,; ; cf. .

la:adj:Terentius.gloss: of or pertaining to the gens Terentia.
senses: of or pertaining to the gens Terentia.
la:adj:Terentius.html:
Tĕrentĭus, i, m.; Tĕrentĭa, ae, f.,
Terence, the name of a Roman gens
P. Terentius After, the celebrated comic poet, born at Carthage A. U. C. 569, ; Ter.—
M. Terentius Varro, a celebrated schotar, an elder contemporary and friend of Cicero, ; .—
C. Terentius Varro, Roman general at Cannœ, .—In fem., Terentia, the wife of Cicero. — Hence,
Tĕ-rentĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Terentius, Terentian: Terentia et Cassia lex frumentaria,. —
Tĕrentĭānus, a, um, adj., of Terence, Terentian: Chremes,i. e. occurring in the poet Terence,; so, Phormio, id. Fragm. ap. : Terentianus ipse se puniens,i. e. the Heautontimoroumenos,: verbum,: exercitus,commanded by M Terentius Varro,.—
Tĕ-rentilla, ae, f.dim. of Terentia, Aug. ap. . —
Subst.: Tĕrentĭā-nus, i, m., a proper name. L. Terentianus Maurus, a grammarian at the close of the first century after Christ, author of a metrical work.

la:verb:tertio.gloss: to do for the third time, thrice
senses: to do for the third time, thrice
la:verb:tertio.html:
tertĭo, no
perf., ātum, 1, v. a.
tertius
, to do for the third time (very rare): jugerum,to plough for the third time,: campos,: colles iterandi tertiandique,: agrum,: tertiata verba, thrice repeated, i. e. stammered out, — Hence, for the third time, thrice: verba tertiato et quartato dicere, Cato ap. .—*
Part.: tertĭātus, a, um, greater by a third: castra,whose length is one third greater than its breadth,.

la:noun:terra.gloss: dry land (as opposed to watery parts of the Earth)
senses: dry land (as opposed to watery parts of the Earth)
ground, floor (the surface of the land)
earth, soil, dirt, clay, clod (the substance generally composing the dry land)
land, country, region, territory (any given area of dry land)
earth (the entire surface of planet Earth; dry land and sea together, as opposed to the heavens)
the Earth, the globe, the world (as a celestial object)
la:noun:terra.html:
terra (archaic tera, ), ae (
gen. terras, Naev. ap. P.: terraï, Enn. ap. ib. (Ann. v. 479 Vahl.); ; ; ; 3, 989 et saep.), f.
perh. Sanscr. root tarsh-, to be dry, thirsty; Lat. torreo, torris; Germ Durst; Engl. thirst; prop. the dry land
, the earth, opp. to the heavens, the sea, the air, etc.; land, ground, soil (cf.: tellus, solum).
In gen.: principio terra universa cernatur, locata in mediā sede mundi, solida et globosa et undique ipsa in sese nutibus suis conglobata, etc.,: terra in medio mundo sita,: hunc statum esse hujus totius mundi atque naturae, rotundum ut caelum, terra ut media sit, eaque suā vi nutuque teneatur,: umbra terrae,: terrae motus,earthquakes,; ; cf. sqq.; : : res invectae ex terrā,: terra continens adventus hostium denuntiat,: Massilia fere ex tribus oppidi partibus mari alluitur: reliqua quarta est, quae aditum habeat a terrā,: cui parti (insulae) nulla est objecta terra,: iter terrā petere,; cf.: ipse terrā eodem pergit,: esse in terrā atque in tuto loco,on solid ground,: ex magnā jactatione terram videns,: terrā marique, by land and by water (very freq.), ; ; Vatin. ap. ; ; cf. : insidiae terrā marique factae,; the form et terrā et mari is also class.,, § 96 (B. and K. bracket the first et); 2, 5, 50, § 131; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; for which also: bellum terrā et mari comparat,: terrā ac mari,: marique terrāque usque quāque quaeritat,: aut terrā aut mari,: mari atque terrā,: mari ac terrā,: mari terrāque,; : natura sic ab his investigata est, ut nulla pars caelo, mari, terrā (ut poëtice loquar) praetermissa sit,: eorum, quae gignuntur e terrā, stirpes et stabilitatem dant iis, quae sustinent, et ex terrā sucum trahunt, etc.,: num qui nummi exciderunt, ere, tibi, quod sic terram Obtuere?: tollere saxa de terrā,: tam crebri ad terram accidebant, quam pira,; so, ad terram,; ; : aliquem in terram statuere,: ne quid in terram defluat,: penitus terrae defigitur arbos,; so. terrae (dat.), ; ; ; ; : sub terris si jura deum,in the infernal regions, (4, 4), 39; cf.: mei sub terras ibit imago,: genera terrae,kinds of earth,: Samia terra,Samian pottery clay,: terrae filius, son of earth, i. e. human being, : terrā orti,natives of the soil, aborigines, autochthones,: cum aquam terramque ab Lacedaemoniis petierunt, water and earth (as a token of subjection), : terram edere,. —
Personified, Terra, the Earth, as a goddess; usu. called Tellus, Magna Mater, Ceres, Cybele, etc.: jam si est Ceres a gerendo, Terra ipsa dea est et ita habetur: quae est enim alia Tellus?; cf. ; ; . 460; ; 140; 152; ; . —
In partic., a land, country, region, territory (cf.: regio, plaga, tractus): Laurentis terra, Enn. ap. P. (Ann. v. 35 Vahl.): terra erilis patria,. 2, 2; cf.: in nostrā terrā in Apuliā,: tua,: mea,: in hac terrā,: in eā terrā (sc. Sicilia),: terra Gallia,: terra Italia, 7, 4 Drak. N. cr.; 29, 10, 5; 30, 32, 6; 38, 47 6; 39, 17, 2; 42, 29, 1: Africa, Hispania, : Pharsalia,. —In plur.: in quascumque terras,: eae terrae,: qui terras incolunt eas, in quibus, etc.,: abire in aliquas terras,: (Cimbri) alias terras petierunt, et saep. — Esp., terrae, the earth, the world: pecunia tanta, quanta est in terris,in the whole earth, in the world,: quid erat in terris, ubi, etc.,; ; ; : ruberes Viveret in terris te si quis avarior,; ; so, aureus hanc vitam in terris Saturnus agebat,: terrarum cura,. — Ante-class., also in terrā, in the world: quibus nunc in terrā melius est?: scelestiorem in terrā nullam esse alteram,; ; ; ; ; .—Hence also the phrase orbis terrarum, the world, the whole world, all nations: quae orbem terrarum implevere famā,: Graecia in toto orbe terrarum potentissima,: cujus tres testes essent totum orbem terrarum nostro imperio teneri,; but freq. also orbis terrarum, the world, i. e. the empire of Rome: orbis terrarum gentiumque omnium,; cf. ; while orbis terrae,the globe, the earth, the world,; ; ; ; but also with ref. to the Roman dominion,; ; ; ; id. Off, 2, 8, 27; ; cf. of the Senate: publicum orbis terrae consilium,; ; ; ; ; v. orbis: quoquo hinc asportabitur terrarum, certum est persequi,: ubi terrarum esses, ne suspicabar quidem, in what country, or where in the world, , so, ubi terrarum, : ubicumque terrarum,; .

la:noun:Tereus.html:
Tēreus, ĕi or ĕos, m., = Τηρεύς.
A king of Thrace, husband of Procne, the sister of Philomela, whom he violated, ; ; . 615; 6, 635; .—Hence, Tērĕĭdes, ae, m., the offspring of Tereus, i. e. his son Itys, .—
The name of a tragedy by Attius, ; .

senses: three as understood symbolically in a cultural context
la:adv:ter.html:
tĕr, adv. num.
Sanscr. tris; Gr. τρίς; cf. tres
,
three times, thrice.
Lit.: ter sub armis malim vitam cernere, quam semel modo parere, Enn. ap. Müll. (Trag. v. 297 Vahl.): haec rude misceto ter in die,: ter in anno,: ter in anno audire nuntium,: ter aut quater die perfricari,: is de se ter sortibus consultum dicebat,: ter aevo functus senex (Nestor),; cf.: ter amplus Geryon,tripleheaded,: pepulisse Ter pede terram,; 4, 1, 28; : ter consul,: ter in annum tesseras dare, et saep.—With numerals: ter quattuor corpora, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 96 Vahl.): ter quinquagenos sues habere,; cf.: terni ter cyathi,; and: ter centena epigrammata,: ter centum milibus,; so, ter centum (by many written as one word, tercentum),; : ter denis redeuntibus annis,: ter denas vaccas Accipit,: ter deno bove,: ter et viciens volneratus est,.—
Transf., in gen., for an indefinite number, = often or repeatedly: ter sese attollens cubitoque annixa levavit: Ter revoluta toro est,: ter si resurgat murus aëneus, ter pereat meis Excisus Argivis; ter uxor Capta virum puerosque ploret,: Aeneam magnā ter voce vocavit,; ; ; : ter tanto pejor ipsa est,: ludos apparat ... stulte bis terque,; so, bis terque,; ; ; : bisque terque,: terque quaterque manu pectus percussit,; so, terque quaterque,: ter et quater,.—
Esp., with adjj., to denote a high degree: felices ter et amplius, quos, etc.,: o ego ter felix, si, etc.,thrice happy, thrice fortunate,: o terque quaterque beati!: o mihi felicem terque quaterque diem,.

la:num:ternus.gloss: three each; three at a time
senses: three each; three at a time

la:verb:terreo.html:
terrĕo, ŭi, ĭtum, 2, v. a.
Sanscr. root tras-, trasāmi, tremble; Gr. τρέω
,
to frighten,

affright, put in fear or dread, to alarm, terrify.

Lit. (class. and very freq.): nec me ista terrent,: adversarios,: qui urbem totam . . . caede incendiisque terreret,: eum hominem istis mortis aut exsilii minis,: suae malae cogitationes terrent,: maris subita tempestas terret navigantes,: milites . . . alii se abdere, pars territos confirmare,: multum ad terrendos nostros valuit clamor,: mortis metu territi,; : aliquem proscriptionis denuntiatione,: metu poenāque,: ut in scenā videtis homines consceleratos impulsu deorum terreri Furiarum taedis ardentibus,: terrere metu,: territus hoste novo,. — With ne and subj.: Samnites maxime territi, ne ab altero exercitu integro intactoque fessi opprimerentur,: terruit urbem, Terruit gentes, grave ne rediret Saeculum Pyrrhae,—With gen.: territus animi, Dietsch; .—Absol.: ut ultro territuri succlamationibus, concurrunt,.—
Transf.
To drive away by terror, to frighten or scare away (poet.): profugam per totum terruit orbem,: fures vel falce vel inguine,; cf.: has (Nymphas) pastor fugatas terruit,: volucres (harundo),: saepe etiam audacem fugat hoc terretque poëtam,: terret ambustus Phaethon avaras Spes,.—
To deter by terror, to scare, frighten from any action: aliquem metu gravioris servitii a repetendā libertate, Dietsch: ut, si nostros loco depulsos vidisset, quo minus libere hostes insequerentur, terreret,.—With ne, ; : memoria pessimi proximo bello exempli terrebat, ne rem committerent eo,: praesentiā tuā, ne auderent transitum, terruisti, Auct. Pan. ap. Constant. 22: non territus ire,: inimicos loqui terrent amplitudine potestatis,.

la:noun:terror.gloss: a dread, terror, great fear, alarm, panic
senses: a dread, terror, great fear, alarm, panic
an object of fear or dread
la:noun:terror.html:
terror, ōris, m.
terreo
,
great fear, affright, dread, alarm, terror (syn.: pavor, trepidatio, metus).
Lit.: definiunt terrorem metum concutientem: ex quo fit, ut pudorem rubor, terrorem pallor et tremor et dentium crepitus consequatur,: eadem nos formido timidas terrore impulit,; cf.: terrorem alicui inicere,: ferae, injecto terrore mortis horrescunt,: aliquem terrore periculoque mortis repellere,: si Antonio patuisset Gallia ... quantus rei publicae terror impenderet,: alicui terrorem inferre,; ; : reddit inlatum antea terrorem,: teneri terrore,: esse terrori alicui,: qui modo terrori fuerant,: tantus terror incidit exercitui, ut, etc.,: tantus repente terror invasit, ut, etc.,: Romanos auxiliares tyranni in terrorem ac tumultum conjecerunt,: sic terrore oblato a ducibus,: tantum Romae terrorem fecere, ut, etc.,: tantumque terrorem incussere patribus, ut, etc.,: si tantus habet mentes et pectora terror,: volgi pectora terror habet,: terrore pavens,: in oppido festinatio et ingens terror erat, ne, etc., Dietsch: ingentem Galli terrorem memoriā pristinae cladis attulerant,: terror nominis Alexandri invaserat orbem,: arcanus terror,secret dread, secret awe,: exsurgite, inquit, qui terrore meo occidistis prae metu,from dread of me,; cf.: de terrore suo, Auct. B. Afr. 32, 1: saepe totius anni fructus uno rumore periculi atque uno belli terrore amittitur, dread or apprehension of war, : nullum terrorem externum esse,i. e. dread of foreign enemies,; cf.: peregrinus terror,: terror servilis, ne suus cuique domi hostis esset,dread of the slaves,: in omnem terrorem vultum componens,into frightful expressions,: (Periclis) vis dicendi terrorque, terrible power, δεινὁτης, . — Plur.: feri lugubresque terrores,. —
Transf., concr., an object of fear or dread, a terror (usu. in plur.): duobus hujus urbis terroribus depulsis,; cf.: terrores reipublicae (sc. Carthago ac Numantia),: terrores Romani nominis, Treb. Poll. ; : non mediocres terrores jacit atque denuntiat,; cf.: Battonius miros terrores ad me attulit Caesarianos,.—Sing.: Xerxes, terror ante gentium,: Dionysius gentium quondam terror,.

la:noun:tergum.html:
tergum, i (poet. and in post-Aug. prose also tergus, ŏris), n. (
masc.: familiarem tergum,; cf. ) [cf. Gr. τράχηλος, neck; perh. root τρέχω, to run], the back of men or beasts (syn. dor sum).
Lit.
Form tergum: dabitur pol supplicium mihi de tergo vestre,: vae illis virgis miseris quae hodie in tergo morientur meo,: manibus ad tergum rejectis, Asin ap. : boum terga,; cf. tergo poenae pendere : tergo ac capite puniri, Liv 3, 55, 14.—Of cranes eaeque in tergo praevolantium Colla reponunt, 49, 125. — Of the dolphin, Ov F 2, 113.— Of the crocodile: ejus terga cataphracta,.—
Form tergus aurea quam molli tergore vexit ovis, (3, 21), 6: ut equa facilem sui tergoris ascensum praebeat,.—
Transf.
The back or hinder part, the back, rear,
Esp. in the phrases terga vertere or dare, to turn the back, pregn., for to take to flight, to flee: omnes hostes terga verterunt; neque prius fugere destiterunt, quam, etc.,; so, terga vertere,; 3, 21; ; and even of a single person: terga vertit,: qui plures simul terga dederant, etc., Liv 22, 29, 5: terga dare,: inter duas acies Etrusci, cum in vicem his atque illis terga darent,; : terga fugae praebere,: terga praestare (fugae),; . — Trop. jam felicior aetas Terga dedit, tremuloque gradu venit aegra senectus, Ov M. 14, 143.—
In gen.: inflexo mox dare terga genu,i. e. yield to the burden, (4, 8), 6: praebere Phoebo

terga, to sun itself, : concurrit ex insidiis versisque in Lucretium Etruscis terga caedit,the rear,; : terga Parthorum dicam,the flight,: terga collis,; cf.: terga vincentium,: summi plena jam margine libri Scriptus et in tergo necdum finitus Orestes,written on the back,: retro atque a tergo,behind one,; cf.: a tergo, a fronte, a lateribus tenebitur,: ut a tergo Milonem adorirentur,behind,; ; : tumultum hostilem a tergo accepit,; ; ; ; : post tergum hostium legionem ostenderunt,: ne nostros post tergum adorirentur,: Germani post tergum clamore audito,: post tergum hostem relinquere,: qui jam post terga reliquit Sexaginta annos,has left behind him, has passed,: omnia jam diutino bello exhausta post tergum sunt,: omnia, quae post tergum erant, strata,: tot amnibus montibusque post tergum objectis,.—

The back of any thing spread out horizontally, as land or water, i. e. the surface (poet.): proscisso quae suscitat aequore terga,: crassa,: amnis,; ; ; .—
(Pars pro toto.) The body of an animal (poet.).
Form tergum: (serpens) Squamea convolvens sublato pectore terga,; so of a serpent,; Petr 89; of Cerberus,: horrentia centum Terga suum,i. e. a hundred head of swine,: nigrantis terga juvencos,: perpetui tergo bovis,.—
Form tergus: resecat de tergore (suis) partem,of a chine of bacon,: diviso tergore (juvenci),: squalenti tergore serpens,.—
The covering of the back, the skin, hide, leather, etc. (in this signif. tergus freq. occurs; syn.: pellis, corium).
Form tergum: taurino quantum possent circumdare tergo,ox-hide,: ferre novae nares taurorum terga recusant,.—
Form tergus: tergora deripiunt costis et viscera nudant,; so ; med.: durissimum dorso tergus,; cf. ; —
Transf., a thing made of hide or leather.
Form tergum: venti bovis inclusi tergo, i. e. in a bag made of a bull's hide, ; : et feriunt molles taurea terga manus,i. e. tymbals,; so : Idae terga,: pulsant terga,: rupit Terga novena boum, i. e. the nine thicknesses of bull's hide, : tergum Sulmonis,; ; ; hence even: per linea terga (scuti), (v. the passage in connection): duroque intendere bracchia tergo, i. e. cestus,; so .—
Form tergus: gestasset laevā taurorum tergora septem,a shield covered with seven layers of hide,: Martis tergus Geticum,.

la:verb:tergo.gloss: to rub, wipe, wipe off, clean, cleanse

la:verb:termino.gloss: to mark off (by boundaries), set bounds to; bound, limit
senses: to mark off (by boundaries), set bounds to; bound, limit
la:verb:termino.html:
termĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
terminus
,
to set bounds to, mark off by boundaries, to bound, limit (class.; syn.: finio, definio).
Lit.: terra mare et contra mare terras terminat omnes,: fines,; cf.: quorum alter fines vestri imperii non terrae sed caeli regionibus terminaret,: locus, quem oleae terminabant,: quo (lituo) regiones vineae terminavit,: fana,: stomachus palato extremo atque intimo terminatur,: pars prior (togae) mediis cruribus optime terminatur, et saep.: agrum publicum a privato,; .—Absol.: (praetores) terminari jussi, quā ulterior citeriorve provincia servaretur,: famam qui terminet astris,.—
Trop., to limit, set limits to; to circumscribe, fix, define, determine: isdem finibus gloriam, quibus vitam,: quibus regionibus vitae spatium circumscriptum est, eisdem omnes cogitationes suas terminare,: spem possessionum Janiculo et Alpibus,: sonos vocis paucis litterarum notis,: quod ipsa natura divitias, quibus contenta sit et parabiles et terminatas habet,; cf.: victu atque cultu terminatur pecuniae modus,: modum magnitudinis et diuturnitatis,: qui (Epicurus) bona voluptate terminaverit, mala dolore,: summam voluptatem omnis privatione doloris,: ea (lingua) vocem fingit et terminat,: ut subjectos campos terminare oculis haud facile queas,i. e. reach the limits,: gloriam tantam futuram, ut terminari nullo tempore oblivione possit,: prooemia intra quattuor sensus,.—
Transf., to set bounds to, to close, finish, end, terminate: sententiam numerose,: clausulas longa syllaba,; cf.: ut pariter extrema terminentur,: ut, unde est orsa, in eo terminetur oratio,: si, ut Maecenas, etc., dicerentur, genitivo casu non e litterā sed tis syllabā terminarentur,: jam imperio annuo terminato,: si negotium terminatum est,: rem judicio,: litem,.—Hence, adv.: termĭnātē, with limits, Auct. Cas. Lit. Goes. p. 243.

perh. Sanscr. root tarsh-, to be dry, thirsty; Lat. torreo, torris; Germ Durst; Engl. thirst; prop. the dry land
, the earth, opp. to the heavens, the sea, the air, etc.; land, ground, soil (cf.: tellus, solum).

Personified, Terra, the Earth, as a goddess; usu. called Tellus, Magna Mater, Ceres, Cybele, etc.: jam si est Ceres a gerendo, Terra ipsa dea est et ita habetur: quae est enim alia Tellus?; cf. ; ; . 460; ; 140; 152; ; . —
In partic., a land, country, region, territory (cf.: regio, plaga, tractus): Laurentis terra, Enn. ap. P. (Ann. v. 35 Vahl.): terra erilis patria,. 2, 2; cf.: in nostrā terrā in Apuliā,: tua,: mea,: in hac terrā,: in eā terrā (sc. Sicilia),: terra Gallia,: terra Italia, 7, 4 Drak. N. cr.; 29, 10, 5; 30, 32, 6; 38, 47 6; 39, 17, 2; 42, 29, 1: Africa, Hispania, : Pharsalia,. —In plur.: in quascumque terras,: eae terrae,: qui terras incolunt eas, in quibus, etc.,: abire in aliquas terras,: (Cimbri) alias terras petierunt, et saep. — Esp., terrae, the earth, the world: pecunia tanta, quanta est in terris,in the whole earth, in the world,: quid erat in terris, ubi, etc.,; ; ; : ruberes Viveret in terris te si quis avarior,; ; so, aureus hanc vitam in terris Saturnus agebat,: terrarum cura,. — Ante-class., also in terrā, in the world: quibus nunc in terrā melius est?: scelestiorem in terrā nullam esse alteram,; ; ; ; ; .—Hence also the phrase orbis terrarum, the world, the whole world, all nations: quae orbem terrarum implevere famā,: Graecia in toto orbe terrarum potentissima,: cujus tres testes essent totum orbem terrarum nostro imperio teneri,; but freq. also orbis terrarum, the world, i. e. the empire of Rome: orbis terrarum gentiumque omnium,; cf. ; while orbis terrae,the globe, the earth, the world,; ; ; ; but also with ref. to the Roman dominion,; ; ; ; id. Off, 2, 8, 27; ; cf. of the Senate: publicum orbis terrae consilium,; ; ; ; ; v. orbis: quoquo hinc asportabitur terrarum, certum est persequi,: ubi terrarum esses, ne suspicabar quidem, in what country, or where in the world, , so, ubi terrarum, : ubicumque terrarum,; .

la:verb:tero.html:
tĕro, trīvi, trītum, 3 (
perf. terii, acc. to P.; perf. sync. tristi, ), v. a.
root ter; Gr. τείρω, τρύω, τρίβω, to rub; cf. Lat. tribulare, triticum; akin to τέρην, tender, Lat. teres
, to rub, rub to pieces; to bruise, grind, bray, triturate (syn.: frico, tundo, pinso).
Lit. (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose).
In gen.: num me illuc ducis, ubi lapis lapidem terit? (i. e. into a mill), : lacrimulam oculos terendo vix vi exprimere,: teritur lignum ligno ignemque concipit attritu,. § 208: sed nihil hederā praestantius quae

teritur, lauro quae terat, : aliquid in mortario,: aliquid in farinam,: bacam trapetis,: unguibus herbas,: dentes in stipite,: lumina manu,: sucina trita redolent,: piper,: Appia trita rotis,: cibum in ventre,i. e. to digest,med. — Poet.: labellum calamo, i. e. to rub one's lip (in playing), : calcemque terit jam calce Diores,treads upon,: crystalla labris,.—

In partic.
To rub grain from the ears by treading, to tread out, thresh: frumentum,: milia frumenti tua triverit area centum,: area dum messes teret,: teret area culmos,; cf.: ut patria careo, bis frugibus area trita est,i. e. it has twice been harvest-time,.—
To cleanse or beautify by rubbing, to smooth, furbish, burnish, polish, sharpen (syn.: polio, acuo): oculos,: crura mordaci pumice,: hinc radios trivere rotis,smoothed, turned,: vitrum torno,: catillum manibus,: tritus cimice lectus,.—
To lessen by rubbing, to rub away; to wear away by use, wear out: (navem) ligneam, saepe tritam,: hoc (tempus) rigidas silices, hoc adamanta terit,. 14: ferrum,to dull,: mucronem rubigine silicem liquore, (3, 20), 15: trita labore colla,: trita subucula,: trita vestis,: librum,i. e. to read often,; ; cf.: quid haberet, Quod legeret tereretque viritim publicus usus?: pocula labris patrum trita,: ut illum di terant, qui primum olitor caepam protulit, crush, annihilate, Naev. ap. P.—
Of persons, pass., to be employed in. occupied with: nos qui in foro verisque litibus terimur,: litibus,.—
To tread often, to visit, frequent a way or place (cf.: calco, calcito): angustum formica terens iter,: iter propositum, (3, 28), 14: Appiam mannis,: viam,; : via trita pede,: ambulator porticum terit,: limina,: mea nocturnis trita fenestra dolis,nec jam clarissimorum virorum receptacula habitatore servo teruntur,: flavaeque terens querceta Maricae Liris, Claud. Cons. Prob. et Olybr 259. —
In mal. part.: Bojus est, Bojam terit,; so (4. 10), 30; . —
Trop. (freq. in good prose).
To wear away, use up, i. e. to pass, spend time; usu. to waste, spend in dissipation, etc. (syn.: absumo, consumo): teritur dies,: diem sermone terere segnities merast,: naves diem trivere,: tempus in convivio luxuque,: tempus ibi in secreto,: omnem aetatem in his discendis rebus,: teretur interea tempus,: jam alteram aetatem bellis civilibus,: omne aevum ferro,: spe otia,: otium conviviis comissationibusque inter se,. —
To expend, employ (late Lat.): qui operam teri frustra,. —
To exert greatly, exhaust: ne in opere longinquo sese tererent, Liv 6, 8, 10: ut in armis terant plebem,.—
Of language, to wear out by use, i. e. to render common, commonplace, or trite (in verb finit. very rare, but freq. as a P. a.): jam hoc verbum satis hesterno sermone trivimus,: quae (nomina) nunc consuetudo diurna trivit,.—*
To tread under foot, i. e. to injure, violate a thing: jurata deorum majestas teritur,. — Hence, P. a.: trītus, a, um.
Prop. of a road or way, oft-trodden, beaten, frequented, common: iter,: via,: quadrijugi spatium,. — Sup.: tritissima quaeque via,. —
Fig.
Practised, expert: tritas aures habere,; so .—Comp.: tritiores manūs ad aedificandum perficere,. —
Of language, used often or much, familiar, common, commonplace, trite: quid in Graeco sermone tam tritum atque celebratum est, quam, etc.,: nomen minus tritum sermone nostro,: ex quo illud: summum jus summā injuriā factum est jam tritum sermone proverbium,.—Comp.: faciamus tractando usitatius hoc verbum ac tritius,: compedes, quas induere aureas mos tritior vetat,.

la:verb:tergiversor.gloss: to seek an evasion, to tergiversate
senses: to seek an evasion, to tergiversate
la:verb:tergiversor.html:
tergĭ-versor, ātus, 1,
v. dep. n. [ter gum], to turn one's back; hence, to decline refuse; to boggle, shuffle, seek a shift or eva sion; to shift, tergiversate (a favorite word of Cicero; otherwise rare): itaque eam ter giversari non sinent secumque rapient,: an cuncter et tergiverser, ut lis me dem, qui, etc.,: quid taces? quid dissimulas? quid tergiversaris?: hunc aestuantem et tergiversantem judicio ille persequitur, id Fl. 20, 47. Fannius invitus et huc atque il luc tergiversans,; id : quid tergiversamur? in his tribus generibus non incal lide tergiversantur, : non est locus ad tergiversandum,: consules ipsos tergiversari, : movebant consulem haec, sed tergiversari res cogebat,: accusatores aut ca lumniantur aut praevaricantur aut tergi versantur...Tergiversari, in universum ab accusatione desistere. .— Hence, tergiversanter, adv., back wardly, reluctantly: pugnam inire,.
